wajo24_q1.solution:
Let $O$ be the centre of the hexagon.
Diagonals $A D, B E$ and $C F$, pass through $O$ and partition $A B C D E F$ into six congruent equilateral triangles, each of area $24 / 6=4$.
Observe that $B D$ partitions each of $\triangle B C O$ and $\triangle C D O$ into two triangles of equal area.
$$ \begin{aligned} \therefore|A B D| & =|A B O|+|O B D| \\ & =|A B O|+|C B O| \\ & =4+4 \\ & =8. \end{aligned} $$
Alternatively, drop perpendicular from $O$ to $X$ on $A B$. Then $O X$ partitions $\triangle A B O$ into two smaller congruent triangles, so that now $\triangle A D B$ is partitioned by $O X, O B$ and $O C$ into four triangles congruent to $O A X$, i.e.
$$ \begin{aligned} |A B D| & =4|O A X| \\ & =4 \cdot \frac{1}{2} \cdot|A B O| \\ & =8. \end{aligned} $$

wajo24_q3.solution:
Let $m, w$ be the numbers of men and women, respectively, at the start of the party. Then (1) and (2) follow from the given information:
\begin{align*}3(w-15) & =m \tag{1}\\7(m-40) & =w-15 \tag{2}\\\therefore 21(m-40) & =m \\20 m & =21 \cdot 40 \\m & =42 \\\therefore 7(42-40) & =w-15 \\w & =14+15 \\& =29.\end{align*}
Therefore, originally there were 29 women (and 42 men).

f{Alternatively}, working backwards, let $x$ be the number of men remaining after 40 of them have left the party.
Then the number of the women, after 15 women left the party, is $7 x$.
So, the total number of the men at the start of the party is
$$\begin{aligned}3(7 x) & =x+40 \\\therefore 20 x & =40 \\x & =2.\end{aligned}$$
Hence, the number of women at the start of the party was
$$\begin{aligned}7 x+15 & =7 \cdot 2+15 \\& =29.\end{aligned}$$

wajo24_q5.solution:
Let the common difference be $\Delta$. Then
$$ \begin{aligned} 5 \Delta & =339-146 \\ & =193 \\ a & =146+\Delta \\ b & =146+2 \Delta \\ c & =146+3 \Delta \\ d & =146+4 \Delta \\ a+b+c+d & =4 \cdot 146+10 \Delta \\ & =4 \cdot 146+2 \cdot 193 \\ & =584+386 \\ & =970 \end{aligned} $$
Alternatively, with $\Delta$ as above,
$$ \begin{aligned} a & =146+\Delta \\ b & =146+2 \Delta \\ c & =339-2 \Delta \\ d & =339-\Delta \\ \therefore a+b+c+d & =2(146+339) \\ & =2 \cdot 485 \\ & =970. \end{aligned} $$

wajo24_q6.solution:
Let $n$ be a lightweight number less than 100.
Suppose $n$ has one digit, then its digit sum and digit product are the same $\unicode{x21af}$.
So, in fact, $n$ cannot have one digit.
Therefore, $n$ has two digits. Let those digits (in some order) be $a, b$ where $a \leqslant b$.
Consider cases according to $a$.
Case 1: $a \geqslant 2$. Then
$$\begin{aligned}a b & \geqslant 2 b \\\ & \geqslant a+b\unicode{x21af}\end{aligned}$$
So there are no such lightweight numbers.
Case 2: $a=1$. Then
$$\begin{aligned} a b & =b \\\ & <1+b=a+b. \end{aligned}$$
So all such numbers, namely $11,12, \ldots, 19$ together with $21,31, \ldots, 91$ ( $9+8=17$ of them) are lightweight.
Case 3: $a=0$. Then $a$ is necessarily the second digit, and $b$ is necessarily non-zero, and
$$\begin{aligned}a b & =0 \\\ & \ <0+b=a+b\end{aligned}$$
so that, again, all such numbers, namely $10,20, \ldots, 90$ ( 9 of them) are lightweight.
Thus, in total there are $9+8+9=26$ lightweight numbers below 100.
Alternatively, let $n$ be a lightweight number less than 100.
Suppose $n$ has one digit, then its digit sum and digit product are the same $\unicode{x21af}$.
So, in fact, $n$ must have two digits.
Let $n=\overline{a b}$ be its decimal digit representation. Then
$$\begin{aligned}a b & \lt a+b \\\ \therefore (a-1)(b-1) & \lt 1 \end{aligned}$$
Therefore, one of $a, b$ is at most 1.
Hence the possibilities are:
$10,11, \ldots, 19$ (10 possibilities),
$20,30, \ldots, 90$ (8 possibilities),
$21,31, \ldots, 91$ (8 possibilities),
which, in all, is 26 possibilities.

wajo24_q7.solution:
After the price increase the price of the calculator (in dollars) became $200(1+x / 100)$.
Then the price reduced $x \%$ during the sale so that the price is now
$$ \begin{aligned} 182 & =200(1+x / 100)(1-x / 100) \\ & =200(1+y)(1-y), \text{ substituting } y \text{ for } x / 100 \\ & =200\left(1-y^{2}\right) \\ & =200-200 y^{2} \\ \therefore 200 y^{2} & =200-182 \\ & =18 \\ y^{2} & =0.09 \\ x / 100=y & =0.3 \\ x & =30. \end{aligned} $$

$$ \begin{aligned} & \triangle C B Y \cong \triangle A D X, \text{ by AAS: } \angle B=\angle D, \text{ alt. angles } \\ & \angle X=\angle Y=90^{\circ} \\ & C B=A D \\ & \sim \triangle B D A, \text{ by AA: } \angle D \text{ common } \\ & \angle X=\angle A=90^{\circ}. \end{aligned} $$
Also observe that $A D: A B=105: 140=3: 4$, so that $\triangle A D B$ is a $3: 4: 5$ right triangle scaled by 35, giving $B D=5 \cdot 35$. Hence
$$ \begin{aligned} \frac{D X}{A D} & =\frac{D A}{B D} \\ & =\frac{A D}{B D} \\ \therefore D X & =\frac{A D^{2}}{B D} \\ \therefore X Y & =B D-2 D X \\ & =5 \cdot 35-\frac{2(3 \cdot 35)^{2}}{5 \cdot 35} \\ & =7\left(5^{2}-2 \cdot 3^{2}\right) \\ & =49. \end{aligned} $$
Alternatively, after having observed $A D: A B=3: 4$, with the similarities,
$$ \triangle C B Y \sim \triangle A D X \sim \triangle B D A $$
we have,
$$ \begin{aligned} Y B: Y C: C B & =X D: X A: A D=A D: A B: B D=3: 4: 5 \\ \therefore X Y & =B D-X D-Y B \\ & =\frac{5}{3} \cdot A D-\frac{3}{5} \cdot A D-\frac{3}{5} \cdot B C \\ & =\left(\frac{5}{3}-2 \cdot \frac{3}{5}\right) A D \\ & =\frac{5^{2}-2 \cdot 3^{2}}{3 \cdot 5} \cdot 105 \\ & =(25-18) \cdot 7 \\ & =49. \end{aligned} $$

wajo24_q12.solution:
Let $r, R$ be the radii of the small and large circles, respectively.
Let $M$ be the midpoint of $B C$, and let $a$ be the distance from the circles' centre to $M$.
We have $A B=C D=15$ and $B M=M C=\frac{1}{2} \cdot 46=23$. Thus,
$$ \begin{aligned} S & =\pi R^{2}-\pi r^{2} \\ & =\pi\left(R^{2}-r^{2}\right) \\ \therefore S / \pi & =R^{2}-r^{2} \\ & =\left(a^{2}+(15+23)^{2}\right)-\left(a^{2}+23^{2}\right) \\ & =(15+23)^{2}-23^{2} \\ & =(15+23+23)(15+23-23) \\ & =61 \cdot 15 \\ & =915 \end{aligned} $$
Note. The region between two concentric circles is called an annulus.

Alternatively, draw a line through $A$ and the common centre of the circles, meeting the small circle in points $X$ and $Y$. As above, we have $S=\pi\left(R^{2}-r^{2}\right)$ but then use the theorem below.
$$ \begin{aligned} \therefore S / \pi & =R^{2}-r^{2} \\ & =(R-r)(R+r) \\ & =A X \cdot A Y \\ & =A B \cdot A C, \text{ by Theorem } \\ & =15 \cdot(15+46) \\ & =15 \cdot 61 \\ & =915 \end{aligned} $$
Theorem. If two lines through a point $A$ meet a circle $K$ at points $B, C$ and $X, Y$, respectively (see diagram), then
$$ A B \cdot A C=A X \cdot A Y $$
Proof. Since $B X Y C$ is cyclic, its exterior angle at $B$ and interior opposite angle at $Y$ are equal, i.e.
$$ \begin{aligned} \angle A B X & =\angle X Y C \\ & =\angle A Y C, \text{ same angle } \end{aligned} $$
Also, $\angle B A X=\angle Y A C$, same angle
$$ \begin{aligned} \therefore \triangle A B X & \sim \triangle A Y C, \text{ by AA Rule } \\ \therefore \frac{A B}{A X} & =\frac{A Y}{A C} \\ \therefore A B \cdot A C & =A X \cdot A Y \end{aligned} $$
Note. The theorem is true whether the point $A$ is inside or outside of the circle $K$; when $A$ is inside $K$, the theorem is often called the Bowtie Theorem.
Also, one can show that the common value of $A B cdot A C$ and $A X cdot A Y$ depends only on the distance $d$ of $A$ from the centre of $K$ and the radius $r$ of $K$, and this common value,

$$ d^2-r^2, $$
is called the Power of $A$ (relative to circle $K$ ). The astute reader will note that the above value is negative when $A$ is inside $K$, and indeed the Power of $A$ is defined to be negative inside $A$ via a directed segment convention for the line segments $A B$ and $A C$, and for $A X$ and $A Y$.

wajo24_q13.solution:
Identify sets $A, B$ and $C$ with problems $A, B$ and $C$, and let $a, b, c, d, e, f, g \geqslant 0$ be the numbers of contestants solving the problems corresponding to the regions in the Venn Diagram shown, so that, in particular, $a, b$, and $c$ are the numbers of contestants solving $A$ only, $B$ only, and $C$ only, respectively.
Since all 36 contestants solved at least one problem,
\begin{align*} \text{by (i)}, && a+b+c+d+e+f+g &=36. \tag{1} \\ \text{By (ii)}, && b+d &=2(c+d) \\ && \therefore d &=b-2 c, \tag{2} \\ \text{and, in particular}, && b &\geqslant 2 c. \\ \tag{3}\\ \text{By (iv)}, && \frac{a+b+c}{2} &=b+c \\ && \therefore a &=b+c. \tag{4} \\ \text{By (iii)}, && e+f+g &=a-1 \\ && &=b+c-1.\tag{5} \end{align*}
Then, by (1), (4), (2), (5), $(b+c)+b+c+(b-2 c)+(b+c-1)=36$
\begin{align*} 4 b+c & =37 \tag{6}\\ & & \therefore c & \equiv 1 \quad(\bmod 4). \end{align*}
So now, $c=1$ or $c \geqslant 5$.
But $c \geqslant 5$ implies by (6), that $b \leqslant 8$ so that $b<2 c$, contradicting (3).
Therefore, $c=1$ and $b=9$.
Checking the other conditions we have: $a=b+c=10, d=b-2 c=7, e+f+g=a-1=9.

wajo24_q16.solution:
Let $X$ be the centre of the semicircle.
Let $O^{\prime}$ be the centre of the small circle, and $r$ be its radius.
Let $O O^{\prime}$ meet the quarter-circle arc $A B$ at $P$.
Let $Y, W$ be the feet of the perpendiculars dropped from $O^{\prime}$ to $O B, O A$, respectively.
Let $R$ be the radius of the semicircle, so that the radius of the quarter-circle is $2 R$.
Let $x=Y O^{\prime}\left(=O W\right.$, since rightangles at $\angle Y, \angle O$ and $\angle W$, make $Y O W O^{\prime}$ a rectangle, so that also $O Y=r$ ).
Note that where circles touch they have a common tangent.
Consequently, $X O^{\prime}$ passes through the point where the semicircle and small circle touch, and $O, O^{\prime}, P$ are collinear. Hence,
$$ \begin{aligned} x^{2} & =X O^{\prime 2}-X Y^{2} \\ & =(R+r)^{2}-(R-r)^{2} \\ & =4 R r \\ O O^{\prime} & =O P-O^{\prime} P \\ & =2 R-r \end{aligned} $$
Then, $x^{2}+r^{2}=(2 R-r)^{2}$
$$ \begin{aligned} \therefore 4 R r & =(2 R-r)^{2}-r^{2} \\ & =(2 R-2 r) \cdot 2 R \\ \therefore r & =R-r \\ 2 r & =R \\ \therefore r & =\frac{1}{4} \cdot 2 R \\ & =\frac{1}{4} \cdot 92 \\ & =23. \end{aligned} $$
